claim: The macaque brain contains a network of interconnected areas devoted to the processing of faces called the face-patch system, which forms a subsystem of the inferotemporal (IT) cortex.
source: The macaque brain contains a network of interconnected areas devoted to the processing of faces. This network, the face-patch system, forms a subsystem of the inferotemporal (IT) cortex (Tsao et al., 2006; Moeller et al., 2008; Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Hesse and Tsao, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing the existence and organization of the face-patch system.

claim: Neurons across the face-patch network show response selectivity for faces and are organized in face patches that are spatially and functionally distinct modules.
source: Neurons across the network show response selectivity for faces, but are organized in face patches–spatially and functionally distinct modules (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010; Freiwald, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research documenting the organization and selectivity of face patches.

claim: Face patches exhibit an information processing hierarchy from posterior to anterior areas.
source: These patches exhibit an information processing hierarchy from posterior to anterior areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by the subsequent description of processing stages and citations to Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: In the posterior face-patch PL, neurons respond to face components.
source: In the most posterior face-patch, PL (posterior lateral), neurons respond to face components (Issa and DiCarlo, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research on PL neurons.

claim: In face patch ML/MF, neurons respond to whole faces in a view-specific manner.
source: In ML/MF (middle lateral/middle fundus), neurons respond to whole faces in a view-specific manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the face-patch hierarchy and citations to Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: In face patch AL, responses are view-specific but mostly reflection-invariant.
source: In AL (anterior lateral), responses are still view-specific, but mostly reflection-invariant.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the face-patch hierarchy and citations to Freiwald and Tsao, 2010.

claim: In face patch AM, neurons respond with sensitivity to the identity of the face but in a view-invariant fashion.
source: Finally in AM (anterior medial), neurons respond with sensitivity to the identity of the face, but in a view-invariant fashion (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research on AM neurons.

claim: The average neuronal response latencies increase across the sequence of face-patch stages from posterior to anterior.
source: The average neuronal response latencies increase across this particular sequence of stages (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research measuring response latencies.

claim: Visual information is transformed across the face-patch hierarchy in a way that facilitates the recognition of individual faces despite view variations.
source: Thus, it appears as if visual information is transformed across this hierarchy of representational stages in a way that facilitates the recognition of individual faces despite view variations.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the described hierarchical organization and processing properties of the face-patch system.

claim: Feedforward CNNs remain among the best models for predicting mid- and high-level cortical representations of novel natural images within the first 100–200ms after stimulus onset.
source: Feedforward CNNs remain among the best models for predicting mid- and high-level cortical representations of novel natural images within the first 100–200ms after stimulus onset (Yamins et al., 2014; Khaligh-Razavi and Kriegeskorte, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research comparing CNN predictions to neural data.

claim: Diverse CNN models trained on various tasks have been shown to replicate at least some aspects of face-patch system representations.
source: Diverse CNN models, trained on tasks such as face identification (Farzmahdi et al., 2016; Abudarham et al., 2021; Raman and Hosoya, 2020), object recognition (Chang et al., 2021), inverse graphics (Yildirim et al., 2020), sparse coding (Hosoya and Hyvärinen, 2017), and unsupervised generative modeling Higgins et al., 2021 have all been shown to replicate at least some aspects of face-patch system representations.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to research demonstrating CNN models' ability to replicate face-patch representations.

claim: Face-selective artificial neurons occur even in untrained CNNs.
source: Face-selective artificial neurons occur even in untrained CNNs (Baek et al., 2021a), and functional specialization between object and face representation emerges in CNNs trained on the dual task of recognizing objects and identifying faces (Dobs et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research on untrained CNNs.

claim: Neurons in the AL face-patch typically respond with different firing rates to varying views of a face but with similar firing rates to views that are horizontal reflections of each other.
source: Neurons in this region typically respond with different firing rates to varying views of a face (e.g. a lateral profile vs. a frontal view), but they respond with similar firing rates to views that are horizontal reflections of each other (e.g. left and right lateral profiles) (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research characterizing AL neuron responses.

claim: Learning to discriminate among bilaterally symmetric object categories induces reflection-equivariant intermediate representations in CNNs.
source: Learning to discriminate among bilaterally symmetric object categories induces reflection-equivariant intermediate representations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript showing this effect across multiple trained networks.

claim: AL-like mirror-symmetric tuning is achieved when reflection-equivariant responses are spatially pooled by downstream units with sufficiently large receptive fields.
source: AL-like mirror-symmetric tuning is achieved when such equivariant responses are spatially pooled by downstream units with sufficiently large receptive fields.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing the emergence of mirror-symmetric tuning in fully connected layers.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in convolutional neural network models is not unique to faces and emerges for multiple object categories with bilateral symmetry.
source: First, using 3D objects rendered from multiple views as test stimuli, we demonstrate that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in convolutional neural network models is not unique to faces: it emerges for multiple object categories with bilateral symmetry.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2 showing mirror-symmetric tuning across multiple object categories.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can emerge as a consequence of exposure to bilaterally symmetric objects beyond the category of faces.
source: Our theory predicts that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can emerge as a consequence of exposure to bilaterally symmetric objects beyond the category of faces, and that it can generalize beyond previously experienced object categories.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the theoretical framework and experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can generalize beyond previously experienced object categories.
source: Our theory predicts that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning can emerge as a consequence of exposure to bilaterally symmetric objects beyond the category of faces, and that it can generalize beyond previously experienced object categories.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the theoretical framework and experimental results, particularly the finding that networks trained on non-face objects show mirror-symmetric tuning for faces.

claim: Object recognition involves a large portion of cortex and considerable metabolic cost.
source: Although we experience object recognition as immediate and effortless, the process involves a large portion of cortex and considerable metabolic cost (Laughlin et al., 1998), and determining the neural mechanisms and computational principles that enable this ability remains a major neuroscientific challenge.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research on the metabolic cost of neural processing.

claim: Determining the neural mechanisms and computational principles that enable object recognition remains a major neuroscientific challenge.
source: Although we experience object recognition as immediate and effortless, the process involves a large portion of cortex and considerable metabolic cost (Laughlin et al., 1998), and determining the neural mechanisms and computational principles that enable this ability remains a major neuroscientific challenge.
evidence: The claim reflects the current state of knowledge in the field and is supported by the context of the research.

claim: Several species, including humans, confuse lateral mirror images more often than vertical mirror images.
source: Several species, including humans, confuse lateral mirror images (e.g. the letters b and d) more often than vertical mirror images (e.g. the letters b and p; Sutherland, 1960; Todrin and Blough, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to research on mirror image confusion.

claim: Children often experience confusion between lateral mirror images when learning to read and write.
source: Children often experience this confusion when learning to read and write (Nelson and Peoples, 1975; Bornstein et al., 1978; Cornell, 1985; Dehaene et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to research on children's mirror confusion.

claim: Single-cell recordings in macaque monkeys presented with simple stimuli indicate a certain degree of reflection-invariance in IT neurons.
source: Single-cell recordings in macaque monkeys presented with simple stimuli indicate a certain degree of reflection-invariance in IT neurons (Rollenhagen and Olson, 2000; Baylis and Driver, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological research.

claim: Human neuroimaging experiments revealed reflection-invariance across higher-level visual regions for human heads and other bilaterally symmetric objects.
source: Human neuroimaging experiments also revealed reflection-invariance across higher-level visual regions for human heads (Axelrod and Yovel, 2012; Kietzmann et al., 2012; Ramírez et al., 2014; Kietzmann et al., 2017) and other bilaterally symmetric objects (Dilks et al., 2011; Ramírez et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to neuroimaging research.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning has been reported in a small subset of monkeys' STS and IT cells in early recordings.
source: Such tuning has been reported in a small subset of monkeys' STS and IT cells in early recordings (Perrett et al., 1991; Logothetis et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to early electrophysiological research.

claim: fMRI-guided single-cell recordings revealed the prevalence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning among the cells of face patch AL.
source: fMRI-guided single-cell recordings revealed the prevalence of this tuning profile among the cells of face patch AL (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to research using fMRI-guided recordings.

claim: Global spatial pooling is a sufficient condition for the emergence of reflection-invariant responses if the pooled representation is reflection-equivariant.
source: We showed that global spatial pooling is a sufficient condition for the emergence of reflection-invariant responses, if the pooled representation is reflection-equivariant.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing that global average pooling applied to equivariant representations yields reflection-invariant responses.

claim: Equivariance can be driven by the task demand of discriminating among objects that have bilateral symmetry.
source: We also showed that equivariance can be driven by the task demand of discriminating among objects that have bilateral symmetry (see Olah et al., 2020 for an exploration of emergent equivariance using activation maximization).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results from training networks on different datasets (Figure 4) and a citation to related work.

claim: The combined effect of equivariance and pooling leads to a leap in reflection-invariance between the last convolutional layer and the fully connected layers in CNNs.
source: The combined effect of equivariance and pooling leads to a leap in reflection-invariance between the last convolutional layer and the fully connected layers in CNNs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing the increase in mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index at the transition to fully connected layers.

claim: The transition from view-selective cells in face patches ML/MF to mirror-symmetric viewpoint-selective cells in AL may be similar to the transition between convolutional and fully connected layers in CNNs.
source: This transition may be similar to the transition from view-selective cells in face patches ML/MF to mirror-symmetric viewpoint-selective cells in AL.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the similarity between the computational mechanisms in CNNs and the observed neural properties.

claim: In both CNNs and primate cortex, the mirror-symmetrically viewpoint-tuned neurons are a penultimate stage on the path to full view invariance.
source: In both CNNs and primate cortex, the mirror-symmetrically viewpoint-tuned neurons are a penultimate stage on the path to full view invariance (Freiwald and Tsao, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by the hierarchical organization observed in both systems and a citation to neural data.

claim: It is not necessary to train on a specific object category (including faces) in order to acquire reflection equivariance and invariance for exemplars of that category.
source: Here, we show that it is not necessary to train on a specific object category (including faces) in order to acquire reflection equivariance and invariance for exemplars of that category.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing that networks trained on CIFAR-10 (without faces) exhibit mirror-symmetric tuning for faces.

claim: Learning mirror-invariant stimulus-to-response mappings gives rise to equivariant and invariant representations also for novel stimulus classes.
source: Instead, learning mirror-invariant stimulus-to-response mappings gives rise to equivariant and invariant representations also for novel stimulus classes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing generalization of mirror-symmetric tuning to novel object categories.

claim: Training on ImageNet induces equivariance (in convolutional layers) and invariance (in fully connected layers) to the horizontal reflection of most natural images and 3D renders.
source: ImageNet training induces equivariance (in convolutional layers) and invariance (in fully connected layers) to the horizontal reflection of most natural images and 3D renders.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing distributions of equivariance and invariance measures.

claim: The main limitation of the current study is that the findings are simulation-based and empirical in nature and might be limited to the particular design choices shared across the range of CNNs evaluated.
source: The main limitation of the current study is that our findings are simulation-based and empirical in nature. Therefore, they might be limited to the particular design choices shared across the range of CNNs we evaluated.
evidence: This is a self-assessment of the study's limitations by the authors.

claim: CNNs trained to discriminate among bilaterally symmetric categories develop mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning across the visual field.
source: CNNs trained to discriminate among bilaterally symmetric categories develop mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning across the visual field (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in a supplementary figure.

claim: The findings only establish that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning is a viable computational means for achieving view invariance; they do not prove it to be a necessary condition.
source: A second consequence of the simulation-based nature of this study is that our findings only establish that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning is a viable computational means for achieving view invariance; they do not prove it to be a necessary condition.
evidence: This is a self-assessment of the scope of the findings by the authors.

claim: Previous modeling studies have demonstrated that a direct transition from view-specific processing to view invariance is possible.
source: In fact, previous modeling studies Farzmahdi et al., 2016; Leibo et al., 2015; Leibo et al., 2017 have demonstrated that a direct transition from view-specific processing to view invariance is possible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: In practice, both CNNs and the face-patch network adopt solutions that include intermediate representations with mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: However, in practice, we observe that both CNNs and the face-patch network adopt solutions that include intermediate representations with mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental observations in the manuscript and known properties of the face-patch system.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for non-face objects should exist in cortical regions homologous to AL.
source: Extrapolating from the results in CNNs, we hypothesize that mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for non-face objects should exist in cortical regions homologous to AL.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the CNN results, representing a hypothesis for future testing.

claim: The mirror-symmetric tuning of non-face objects does not necessarily have to be previously experienced by the animal.
source: The mirror-symmetric tuning of these objects does not necessarily have to be previously experienced by the animal.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the generalization observed in CNNs.

claim: Recent findings report a functional clustering of IT into four separate networks, each elongated across the IT cortex and consisting of three stages of processing.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the recent findings of Bao et al., 2020. They report a functional clustering of IT into four separate networks. Each of these networks is elongated across the IT cortex and consists of three stages of processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to recent research on IT organization.

claim: The intermediate nodes of the three non-face selective networks in IT have reflection-invariant yet view-selective tuning, analogous to AL's representation of faces.
source: We hypothesize that the intermediate nodes of the three non-face selective networks have reflection-invariant yet view-selective tuning, analogous to AL's representation of faces.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the CNN results and the known organization of IT.

claim: The 3D object stimulus set consists of nine categories (cars, boats, faces, chairs, airplanes, animals, tools, fruits, and flowers) with 25 exemplars each.
source: The combined object set consisted of nine categories (cars, boats, faces, chairs, airplanes, animals, tools, fruits, and flowers). Each category included 25 exemplars.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus set used in the study.

claim: Each object exemplar was rendered from nine views, spanning from –90° (left profile) to +90°, with steps of 22.5°.
source: We rendered each exemplar from nine views, giving rise a total of 2025 images. The views span from –90° (left profile) to +90°, with steps of 22.5°.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimulus set used in the study.

claim: The rendered images were converted to grayscale, placed on a uniform gray background, and scaled to 227 × 227 pixels to match the input image size of AlexNet.
source: The rendered images were converted to grayscale, placed on a uniform gray background, and scaled to 227 × 227 pixels to match the input image size of AlexNet, or to 224 × 224 to match the input image size of the VGG-like network architectures.
evidence: This is a description of the image preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: Mean luminance and contrast of non-background pixels were equalized across images using the SHINE toolbox.
source: Mean luminance and contrast of non-background pixels were equalized across images using the SHINE toolbox (Willenbockel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the image preprocessing methods used in the study.

claim: In an ImageNet-trained AlexNet, horizontal-reflection equivariance increased across convolutional layers.
source: In an ImageNet-trained AlexNet, horizontal-reflection equivariance increased across convolutional layers (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: In an ImageNet-trained AlexNet, invariance jumped from a low level in convolutional layers to a high level in the fully connected layers and was highest for horizontal reflection.
source: In this trained AlexNet, invariance jumped from a low level in convolutional layers to a high level in the fully connected layers and was highest for horizontal reflection, lower for vertical reflection, and lowest for 90° rotation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: In an untrained AlexNet, the reflection equivariance of the first convolutional layer was higher than in the trained network.
source: In an untrained AlexNet, the reflection equivariance of the first convolutional layer was higher than in the trained network.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The higher level of reflection-equivariance of the first layer of the untrained network can be explained by the lack of strongly oriented filters in the randomly initialized layer weights.
source: The higher level of reflection-equivariance of the first layer of the untrained network can be explained by the lack of strongly oriented filters in the randomly initialized layer weights.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of randomly initialized networks.

claim: Training leads to oriented filters in the first layer but also promotes downstream convolutional representations that have greater reflection-equivariance than those in a randomly-initialized, untrained network.
source: While the training leads to oriented filters in the first layer, it also promotes downstream convolutional representations that have greater reflection-equivariance than those in a randomly-initialized, untrained network.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing data from trained and untrained networks in Figure 3.

claim: The gap between horizontal reflection and vertical reflection in terms of both equivariance and invariance was less pronounced in the untrained network.
source: The gap between horizontal reflection and vertical reflection in terms of both equivariance and invariance was less pronounced in the untrained network (Figure 3B), indicating a contribution of task training to the special status of horizontal reflection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The gap between vertical reflection and 90° rotation in terms of both equivariance and invariance was preserved in the untrained network.
source: In contrast, the gap between vertical reflection and 90° rotation in terms of both equivariance and invariance was preserved in the untrained network.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The greater degree of invariance and equivariance for vertical reflection compared to 90° rotation is largely caused by the test images' structure rather than task training.
source: This indicates that the greater degree of invariance and equivariance for vertical reflection compared to 90° rotation is largely caused by the test images' structure rather than task training.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of trained and untrained networks.

claim: Unlike 90° rotation, vertical and horizontal reflection both preserve the relative prevalence of vertical and horizontal edge energy, which may not be equal in natural images.
source: One interpretation is that, unlike 90° rotation, vertical and horizontal reflection both preserve the relative prevalence of vertical and horizontal edge energy, which may not be equal in natural images (Coppola et al., 1998; Torralba and Oliva, 2003; Henderson and Serences, 2021; Girshick et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to research on natural image statistics.

claim: The training-dependent layer-by-layer increase in equivariance and invariance to horizontal reflection was as pronounced for natural images as it was for the rendered 3D object images.
source: The training-dependent layer-by-layer increase in equivariance and invariance to horizontal reflection was as pronounced for natural images as it was for the rendered 3D object images.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing data from Figure 3A and Figure 3C.

claim: The emergent invariance and equivariance under horizontal reflection are not an artifact of the synthetic object stimulus set.
source: Therefore, the emergent invariance and equivariance under horizontal reflection are not an artifact of the synthetic object stimulus set.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the consistency of results across different stimulus sets.

claim: When evaluated on random noise images, the ImageNet-trained AlexNet still showed a slightly higher level of horizontal reflection-equivariance.
source: Repeating these analyses on random noise images, the ImageNet-trained AlexNet still showed a slightly higher level of horizontal reflection-equivariance (Figure 3E), demonstrating the properties of the features learned in the task independently of symmetry structure in the test images.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: When an untrained AlexNet was evaluated on random noise images, the differences between horizontal reflection, vertical reflection, and rotation measures disappeared, and the invariance and equivariance measures were zero.
source: When we evaluated an untrained AlexNet on random noise images (Figure 3F), that is, when there was no structure in either the test stimuli or the network weights, the differences between horizontal reflection, vertical reflection, and rotation measures disappeared, and the invariance and equivariance measures were zero, as expected
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: A high level of reflection-invariance is associated with the layer's pooling size and the reflection-equivariance of its feeding representation.
source: To summarize this set of analyses, a high level of reflection-invariance is associated with the layer's pooling size and the reflection-equivariance of its feeding representation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The pooling size depends only on the architecture, but the reflection-equivariance of the feeding representation depends on both architecture and training.
source: The pooling size depends only on the architecture, but the reflection-equivariance of the feeding representation depends on both architecture and training.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of trained and untrained networks.

claim: Training on recognizing objects in natural images induces a greater degree of invariance and equivariance to horizontal reflection compared to vertical reflection or 90° rotation.
source: Training on recognizing objects in natural images induces a greater degree of invariance and equivariance to horizontal reflection compared to vertical reflection or 90° rotation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The greater invariance and equivariance to horizontal reflection is consistent with the statistics of natural images as experienced by an upright observer looking, along a horizontal axis, at upright bilaterally symmetric objects.
source: This is consistent with the statistics of natural images as experienced by an upright observer looking, along a horizontal axis, at upright bilaterally symmetric objects.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on knowledge of natural image statistics and the ecological context of vision.

claim: Image reflection, in a world ordered by gravity, does not change the category of an object.
source: Image reflection, in such a world ordered by gravity, does not change the category of an object (although rare examples of dependence of meaning on handedness exist, such as the letters p and q, and molecules whose properties depend on their chirality).
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about object categories and symmetry.

claim: A network trained on CIFAR-10 reproduced a considerable level of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces in layers fc1 and fc2.
source: Although this dataset contains no human face images (such images appear coincidentally in the ImageNet dataset, Yang et al., 2022), the CIFAR-10-trained network reproduced the result of a considerable level of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces in layers fc1 and fc2 (Figure 4B, top row).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The CIFAR-10-trained network showed mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for other bilaterally symmetric objects such as cars, airplanes, and boats.
source: This network also showed mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for other bilaterally symmetric objects such as cars, airplanes, and boats (Figure 4C, blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The SVHN-trained network showed a very low level of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces.
source: Unlike the network trained on CIFAR-10, the SVHN-trained network showed a very low level of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The SVHN-trained network's levels of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for cars, airplanes, and boats were reduced relative to the CIFAR-10-trained network.
source: Furthermore, its levels of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for cars, airplanes, and boats were reduced relative to the CIFAR-10-trained network.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: The symSVHN-trained network reproduced the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning observed in the CIFAR-10-trained network.
source: We found that the symSVHN-trained network reproduced the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning observed in the CIFAR-10-trained network.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The asymSVHN-trained network reproduced the low levels of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning observed for the original SVHN dataset.
source: The asymSVHN-trained network reproduced the low levels of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning observed for the original SVHN dataset.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Given the spatial pooling carried out by fc1, the task demand of reflection-invariant recognition is a sufficient condition for the emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces.
source: Together, these results suggest that given the spatial pooling carried out by fc1, the task demand of reflection-invariant recognition is a sufficient condition for the emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning for faces.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results from training networks on different datasets.

claim: Mirror-reflected views of an object induce similar representations because of reflection-equivariant local features rather than global 2D configurations shared between such views.
source: Do mirror-reflected views of an object induce similar representations because of global 2D configurations shared between such views? Or alternatively, are reflection-equivariant local features sufficient to explain the finding of similar responses to reflected views in fc1?
evidence: The claim is supported by the importance mapping analyses presented in Figure 5.

claim: When only the most salient pixels were retained (insertion), the units' mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning levels were similar to those induced by unmodified images.
source: When we retained only the most salient pixels (i.e. insertion), we observed that the units' mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning levels were similar to those induced by unmodified images (Figure 5A–B, dark blue lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Local features highlighted by importance maps are sufficient for generating mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: This result demonstrates that the local features suffice for driving mirror-symmetrically tuned responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the insertion experiment results.

claim: Greying out the most salient pixels (deletion) led to a complete loss of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: Conversely, greying out the most salient pixels (deletion) led to a complete loss of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning (Figure 5A–B, red lines).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Local features highlighted by importance maps are necessary to drive mirror-symmetrically tuned responses.
source: This result demonstrates that the local features are necessary to drive mirror-symmetrically tuned responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the deletion experiment results.

claim: Shuffled images that destroyed global structure while preserving local features largely preserved the units' mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: We found that the shuffled images largely preserved the units' mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: It is the mere presence of a similar set of reflected local features (rather than a reflected global configuration) that explains most of the acquired mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: Thus, it is the mere presence of a similar set of reflected local features (rather than a reflected global configuration) that explains most of the acquired mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the shuffling experiment results.

claim: The fc6 layer learns highly symmetrical weight maps, reducing the sensitivity to local feature configurations and enabling the generation of downstream reflection-invariant representations compared to convolutional layers.
source: The fc6 layer learns highly symmetrical weight maps, reducing the sensitivity to local feature configurations and enabling the generation of downstream reflection-invariant representations compared to convolutional layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: MLMF was more aligned with the CNNs' mid-level representation, notably the last convolutional layers.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Yildirim et al., 2020), MLMF was more aligned with the CNNs' mid-level representation, notably the last convolutional layers (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6A and a citation to previous work.

claim: The AL face patch showed its highest representational alignment with the first fully connected layer.
source: The AL face patch showed its highest representational alignment with the first fully connected layer (Figure 6B), coinciding with the surge of the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index at this processing level (see Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The AM face patch aligned most with the fully connected layers.
source: The AM face patch aligned most with the fully connected layers (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: In the MLMF face patch, reflection-sensitive features contributed more than reflection-invariant ones.
source: In the MLMF face patch, reflection-sensitive features contributed more than reflection-invariant ones, consistent with the dominance of reflection-sensitive information in aligning network layers with MLMF data (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: In the AL and AM face patches, reflection-invariant features accounted for nearly all the observed model–brain RDM correlations.
source: Conversely, in the AL and AM face patches, reflection-invariant features accounted for nearly all the observed model–brain RDM correlations (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: For most of the convolutional layers, the contribution of the reflection-sensitive component to AL or AM alignment was negative.
source: For most of the convolutional layers, the contribution of the reflection-sensitive component to AL or AM alignment was negative—meaning that if the layers' representations were more reflection-invariant, they could have explained the neural data better.
evidence: The claim is supported by the Shapley value analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Replacing fc6 with spatial global average pooling yields a representation with very similar mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning levels.
source: However, replacing fc6 with spatial global average pooling (collapsing each pool5 feature map into a scalar activation) yields a representation with very similar mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Training the network on ImageNet gives rise to a reflection-equivariant representation in pool5.
source: This result is suggestive of an alternative explanation: that training the network on ImageNet gives rise to a reflection-equivariant representation in pool5.
evidence: This is an inference based on the global average pooling experiment results.

claim: If task-training induces approximately reflection-equivariant representations in the deepest convolutional layer of a CNN and approximately uniform pooling in the following fully connected layer, the resulting pooled representation would be approximately reflection-invariant.
source: Therefore, if task-training induces approximately reflection-equivariant representations in the deepest convolutional layer of a CNN and approximately uniform pooling in the following fully connected layer, the resulting pooled representation would be approximately reflection-invariant.
evidence: This is a logical conclusion based on the mathematical properties of equivariance and pooling.

claim: Many object categories in the natural world are bilaterally symmetric with respect to a plane parallel to the axis of gravity and are typically viewed in an upright orientation.
source: Many object categories in the natural world are bilaterally symmetric with respect to a plane parallel to the axis of gravity and are typically viewed (or photographed) in an upright orientation.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge about natural objects and their typical viewing conditions.

claim: Horizontal image reflection tends to yield equally natural images of similar semantic content, whereas vertical reflection and 90° rotation yield unnatural images.
source: Horizontal image reflection, thus, tends to yield equally natural images of similar semantic content, whereas vertical reflection and 90° rotation yield unnatural images.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge about natural image statistics and the effects of different transformations.

claim: All of the categories that show high mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index in fully connected but not convolutional layers have a single plane of symmetry.
source: We found that all of the categories that show high mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index in fully connected but not convolutional layers have a single plane of symmetry.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of 3D object symmetry presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cars and boats have two planes of symmetry: symmetry between their left and right halves and approximate symmetry between their back and front halves.
source: Cars and boats have two planes of symmetry: in addition to the symmetry between their left and right halves, there is an approximate symmetry between their back and front halves.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of 3D object symmetry and visual inspection of the objects.

claim: Quadrilateral symmetry enables mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning even for lower-level representations, such as those in the convolutional layers.
source: Such 3D structure enables mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning even for lower-level representations, such as those in the convolutional layers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cars and boats show high mirror-symmetric tuning in early layers.

claim: Fruits and flowers exhibit radial symmetry but lack discernible symmetry planes, which impedes viewpoint tuning altogether.
source: Fruits and flowers exhibit radial symmetry but lack discernible symmetry planes, a characteristic that impedes viewpoint tuning altogether.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of 3D object symmetry and the low mirror-symmetric tuning observed for these categories.

claim: For an untrained AlexNet, the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index remains relatively constant across the layers.
source: However, for an untrained AlexNet, the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index remains relatively constant across the layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The leap in mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in fc6 is training-dependent.
source: Statistically contrasting mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning between a trained and untrained AlexNet demonstrates that the leap in mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in fc6 is training-dependent (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Shallow and deep convolutional neural network models with varied architectures and objective functions replicate the emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning.
source: Shallow and deep convolutional neural network models with varied architectures and objective functions replicate the emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing results across multiple architectures.

claim: In all convolutional networks evaluated, the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index peaks at the fully-connected or average pooling layers.
source: In all these convolutional networks, the mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index peaks at the fully-connected or average pooling layers.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: ViT, featuring a non-convolutional architecture, does not exhibit mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning peaking at fully-connected or average pooling layers.
source: ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), featuring a non-convolutional architecture, does not exhibit this feature (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: VGGFace, trained on face identification, has a low mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index compared to ImageNet-trained models such as VGG16.
source: Consistent with their findings, our results demonstrate that VGGFace, trained on face identification, has a low mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning index. This is especially notable in comparison to ImageNet-trained models such as VGG16.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The difference between VGG16 and VGGFace can be attributed to the distinct characteristics of their training datasets and objective functions.
source: This difference between VGG16 and VGGFace can be attributed to the distinct characteristics of their training datasets and objective functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of the two networks and their training conditions.

claim: The VGGFace training task consists of mapping frontal face images to identities, which may exclusively emphasize higher-level physiognomic information.
source: The VGGFace training task consists of mapping frontal face images to identities; this task may exclusively emphasize higher-level physiognomic information.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the VGGFace training task and its potential effects on learned representations.

claim: Training on recognizing objects in natural images may result in a more detailed, view-dependent representation compared to training on face identification.
source: In contrast, training on recognizing objects in natural images may result in a more detailed, view-dependent representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the comparison of VGGFace and VGG16 representations.

claim: The average correlation-distance between the fc6 representations of different views of the same face exemplar is 0.70 ± 0.04 in VGGFace and 0.93 ± 0.04 in VGG16 trained on ImageNet.
source: The average correlation-distance between the fc6 representations of different views of the same face exemplar in VGGFace and VGG16 trained on ImageNet. The average correlation-distance between views is 0.70 ± 0.04 in VGGFace and 0.93 ± 0.04 in VGG16 trained on ImageNet.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing the two networks.

claim: The correlation distance between different exemplars depicted from the same view is 0.84 ± 0.14 in VGGFace and 0.58 ± 0.06 in VGG16 trained on ImageNet.
source: The converse correlation distance between different exemplars depicted from the same view is 0.84 ± 0.14 in VGGFace and 0.58 ± 0.06 in VGG16 trained on ImageNet.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing the two networks.

claim: Training on face identification alone may result in representations that cannot explain intermediate levels of face processing.
source: Therefore, as suggested by Yildirim and colleagues, training on face identification alone may result in representations that cannot explain intermediate levels of face processing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of VGGFace and VGG16 and is consistent with previous work.

claim: The similarity of the tuning profiles observed with RSACorr and RSACorrDem is consistent with the interpretation of the emergent mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning as driven by learned equivariant mid-level features rather than low-level stimulus features.
source: The similarity of the tuning profiles observed here and in Figure 2 is consistent with the interpretation of the emergent mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in our models as driven by learned equivariant mid-level features rather than low-level stimulus features.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of different dissimilarity measures presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: Mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in a re-implementation of the Leibo and colleagues model sharply declines for off-center test stimuli.
source: Panels A and B depict how mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in a re-implementation of the Leibo and colleagues model (Leibo et al., 2017) sharply declines for off-center test stimuli.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The same shift in center of the test stimuli has only a negligible effect on mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in AlexNet.
source: In contrast, the same shift in center of the test stimuli has only a negligible effect on mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning in AlexNet (Panel C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: A large proportion of randomly initialized units that meet the Baek et al. selection criterion exhibit markedly asymmetric tuning profiles.
source: However, as this figure illustrates, a large proportion of these units exhibit markedly asymmetric tuning profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Training increased the number of units individually exhibiting mirror-symmetry tuning profiles.
source: Training increased the number of units individually exhibiting mirror-symmetry tuning profiles, as quantified further in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The first fully connected layer shows the most pronounced training-dependent emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning units.
source: The first fully connected layer shows the most pronounced training-dependent emergence of mirror-symmetric viewpoint tuning units, consistent with the findings obtained with the population-level RSA findings described in the main text.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Deeper convolutional layers in various convolutional architectures demonstrated strong alignment with MLMF data, primarily explained by reflection-sensitive features.
source: Deeper convolutional layers in various convolutional architectures demonstrated strong alignment with MLMF data; this alignment is primarily explained by reflection-sensitive features.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In various convolutional architectures, the fully connected and average pooling layers showed notable representational alignment with the AL patch, predominantly explained by features that are invariant to reflection.
source: In various convolutional architectures, the fully connected and average pooling layers showed notable representational alignment with the AL patch. This alignment is predominantly explained by features that are invariant to reflection, rather than those sensitive to reflection.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The deepest layers in different network architectures, with the exception of ViT, show strong representational alignment with the AM face patch, predominantly explained by features that are invariant to reflection.
source: The deepest layers in different network architectures, with the exception of ViT, show strong representational alignment with the AM face patch. This alignment is predominantly explained by features that are invariant to reflection, rather than those sensitive to it.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.
